content.p: On 3 May 2026 more than 22 lakh young people sat India's national medical entrance test, NEET-UG, in pen-and-paper mode at over 5,400 centres. Nine days later the National Testing Agency (NTA) cancelled the whole exam after investigators found that a "guess paper" circulating before the test contained a large share of its actual questions. Candidates sat the exam again on 21 June.

The Central Bureau of Investigation took over the case on 12 May. By late July it had arrested 13 people and filed a charge sheet of about 20,000 pages against them, among them three subject experts that the NTA had appointed to its own paper-setting work. A Delhi court took cognisance of the charge sheet on 12 August. None of the 13 has been tried or convicted; they are accused, and the CBI's allegations are untested in court.
content.h2: A guess paper that was too good
content.p: The trail began with a message. According to Business Today, a Kerala-based MBBS student allegedly sent about 300 "guess paper" questions on the evening of 2 May to his father's phone in Sikar, the Rajasthan coaching town. The accompanying text said they were the questions that would come the next day. The father, who worked at a paying-guest hostel, reportedly handed them to students in the morning without checking them.

Suspicion came only after the exam. A chemistry teacher in Sikar was going through the questions with his students on the night of 3 May when he found that a PDF which had been circulating a day earlier held every chemistry question that had appeared, according to SabrangIndia, along with ninety biology questions. According to The Indian Express, he first approached Sikar police at about 1:30 a.m. on 4 May and emailed the NTA on the evening of 7 May. Business Today reported that the hostel operator also went to Udyog Nagar police station and was allegedly told not to spread rumours.

The Rajasthan Police Special Operations Group (SOG) began questioning students, parents and counsellors. Additional Director General of Police Vishal Bansal said the recovered file ran to about 150 pages and more than 400 questions, and that around 120 of them matched the real paper, including all 90 biology questions and all 45 chemistry questions. SOG Inspector General Ajay Pal Lamba said the accused had allegedly marketed the real paper as a "guess paper" to avoid suspicion, the same report said. SabrangIndia reported that the SOG arrested an alleged mastermind from Dehradun on 7 May, and four NEET aspirants the next day. Police said a counsellor among the five was accused of selling the paper to aspirants as a "guess paper".

Prices reported for the material varied. SabrangIndia put the range at Rs 20,000 to Rs 2 lakh, with some reports as high as Rs 5 lakh, and said copies were allegedly circulating for about Rs 30,000 each the night before the exam. Times of India and police disclosures, cited in one report, said full access to the paper was allegedly sold for Rs 10 lakh to Rs 25 lakh.
content.h2: Cancellation and the CBI takes over
content.p: On 12 May the Department of Higher Education lodged a written complaint, and the CBI registered a first information report the same day, according to the agency. It formed teams of 72 officers and personnel with eight cyber forensic experts and searched 92 locations in Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Haryana, Delhi and other states. That day the NTA cancelled the 3 May exam. SabrangIndia reported that it did so "in the interest of students".

The NTA's own account of the leak was cautious. SabrangIndia reported that on 21 May NTA Director General Abhishek Singh told a parliamentary committee the exam had not been leaked through the agency's system and that officials would use the word "leak" only if the CBI confirmed it.

On 15 May the NTA announced the re-examination for Sunday 21 June, after a meeting at the home of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, Business Today reported. One news report later said the affair became a major political issue and that a protest at Jantar Mantar by a Gen Z group led by the Cockroach Janta Party led to Pradhan's resignation. Telangana Today likewise said he resigned over the row following the protests.
content.h2: Who the CBI says did what
content.p: The first five arrests were made around 12 to 13 May: Shubham Khairnar of Nashik; Mangilal Biwal, his son Vikas and Dinesh Biwal in Jaipur; and Yash Yadav of Gurugram, according to Business Today. A Delhi court sent them to seven days of CBI custody, saying the allegations pointed to an "organised gang" that leaked and circulated confidential exam papers for money. Two more were arrested on 14 May: Dhananjay Lokhande (spelled "Lokhanda" in some reports) from Ahilyanagar and Manisha Waghmare from Pune.

An IANS report described the alleged chain: the paper allegedly came from Lokhande in Ahilyabai Nagar, passed to Khairnar in Nashik, then to Yash Yadav in Haryana, and on to Mangilal and Dinesh Biwal in Rajasthan, who circulated it in Sikar and Jaipur. The same report said investigators believed Sikar was the operational base, and that Yadav and Vikas had studied together at a coaching institute there. It also said the CBI was examining whether relatives of some accused who had cleared NEET were admitted through access to the material. Citing The Print, one report noted that investigating agencies had not publicly alleged wrongdoing against those candidates.

The most serious allegations concern the subject experts. On 16 May a Delhi court sent Prahlad Vitthal Rao Kulkarni and Waghmare to ten days of CBI custody. The CBI described Kulkarni as a chemistry lecturer involved in the examination process on the NTA's behalf with access to the question papers. The agency alleged that in the last week of April, with Waghmare's help, he gathered students for special classes at his Pune home and dictated questions with options and correct answers, which students wrote in notebooks and which "exactly tallied" with the real paper, in the CBI's words. Manisha Gurunath Mandhare, a biology lecturer the NTA appointed as an expert with full access to the botany and zoology papers, was accused of running similar classes in April, dictating leaked questions to students; the CBI's statement on the case said the classes were held at a Pune residence and that most of the questions tallied with the paper.

SabrangIndia reported that the CBI arrested Mandhare on 16 May and Manisha Sanjay Havaldar, the physics expert, on 22 May, and alleged that Havaldar shared physics questions with Mandhare in April. Counsel for Kulkarni and others have opposed the CBI's applications in court; no accused has been reported as pleading guilty.

The CBI filed its charge sheet on Tuesday 28 July 2026 before a special fast-track court. Its spokesperson said it cited 360 witnesses, 422 documents and 43 material objects, and that all 13 charge-sheeted people were in judicial custody. The CBI said its filing included digital forensic reports, handwriting examiners' opinions and academic experts' views on the leaked questions, which it said confirmed the accused's part in circulating them before the exam. Business Today reported that the CBI said it had traced the leak from its source to beneficiary candidates within weeks, and had frozen bank accounts, bank lockers and a demat account.

The 13 named are Kulkarni, Mandhare, Havaldar, Waghmare, Lokhande, Khairnar, Yash Yadav, Mangilal, Vikas and Dinesh Biwal, Dr Manoj Shirure, Tejas Harshad Kumar Shah and Shivraj Raghunath Motegaonkar, according to court reports. The CBI described two of them as associated with coaching institutes who obtained the questions from the experts.

The paperwork itself caused delay. Medical Dialogues reported that the court noted the charge sheet had been filed without a list of documents, and gave the CBI three days to file all annexures because the record ran to around 20,000 pages that had to be scanned and supplied to the accused.

On Wednesday 12 August Special Judge Ajay Gupta took cognisance of the charge sheet. All 13 appeared by video link from Tihar Jail. Telangana Today reported that the judge said there was "overwhelming incriminating material" to prima facie suggest that the 13, including the three experts, formed a syndicate to leak and circulate the paper for illegal gain. Taking cognisance is a step before charges are framed and is not a finding of guilt.

The CBI also applied to investigate further. Its senior public prosecutor V K Pathak told the court on 13 August that fresh digital evidence had emerged and that the agency wanted to examine the role of persons beyond those already accused, according to a report of the hearing. Advocate Hemant Shah, for Kulkarni, argued that the agency cannot investigate further after a charge sheet without express court permission. Counsel for Yash Yadav and Havaldar also opposed it, while the lawyer for Mangilal, Dinesh and Vikas Biwal chose not to. The court also put off arguments on charge after defence lawyers raised objections about the supply of documents.

On Friday 14 August the judge allowed the further investigation, citing fresh digital evidence and reports from the Central Forensic Science Laboratory, Telangana Today reported. The prosecutor told the court that individuals not yet listed as accused needed to be investigated. No later hearing on framing charges, and no bail ruling for the 13, has been reported, so those questions remain open.
content.h2: Re-exam, results and the Supreme Court
content.p: The re-test went ahead on 21 June. The Supreme Court had refused on 17 June to stay it, deferring a plea to a bench led by Justice P S Narasimha, the Tribune reported. In mid-July that bench dismissed one challenge to the cancellation as infructuous because the re-exam had been held, while telling the petitioner to join the pending cases on wider reform, according to Medical Dialogues. The NTA declared results on 16 July. Khaleej Times reported that close to 2 million candidates appeared and 138 scored above 690 out of 720.

The wider litigation concerns the NTA itself. On 29 May the Narasimha bench, as quoted by the Tribune, said accountability required identifying the specific duty bearers. SabrangIndia reported that the NTA told the court on 29 May it would move NEET to digital testing from the next cycle. At a hearing on 18 September, LiveLaw reported, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said a task force headed by Nandan Nilekani had consulted the earlier committee headed by K. Radhakrishnan, and asked for time until the end of September to file an affidavit. Justice Narasimha said the court might visit the NTA's new office on Minto Road to see whether the system works.
For the criminal case, the next steps are the CBI's further investigation, arguments on charge, and any trial. No one has been convicted.
